Foreign-Backed Blockade Disrupts Automotive Plants Across Silesia

A wave of coordinated blockades at several automotive manufacturing sites in Poland’s Silesia region has brought production to a halt, as thousands of workers remain unable to access their workplaces. The protests, which local authorities attribute to the influence of a foreign state, began early Tuesday morning and show no signs of abating.

At the heart of the disruption are five major assembly plants, including the large-scale facilities operated by Motopol and Vistula Auto, which together employ more than 8,000 workers. Protesters have erected barricades at main entrances, preventing employees from entering and halting vehicle production lines.

“Everything stopped at 6 a.m. when we arrived and found the gates blocked,” said Marek Kwiatkowski, a line supervisor at the Motopol factory in Gliwice. “Our entire shift waited outside, but no one could go in.” Workers have been told to remain at home or stay offsite until further notice.

The Silesian Automotive Association has condemned the blockade, warning of significant losses for the region’s automotive sector. “We estimate that the stoppage is costing our members millions of zlotys each day in lost output,” said Dr. Anna Przybysz, the association’s spokesperson. “This comes at a crucial time, as order books are full and production was scheduled to ramp up for the summer.”

Local police report that the protesters are well-organized, with banners and supplies set up outside each facility. Authorities allege that the blockade has been instigated and coordinated with support from outside Poland, though have provided no further details on the foreign state involved.

Union representatives have voiced concern for workers’ livelihoods. “Our members are worried about their jobs and pay,” said Tomasz Zielinski, chair of the United Auto Workers of Silesia. “We call for a peaceful resolution and immediate reopening of the plants.”

As the blockade enters its second day, automotive companies are assessing the impact on their operations. Some report that completed vehicles are unable to leave storage lots, while unfinished cars remain idle on assembly lines. At present, there is no indication of when the blockades will be lifted, leaving thousands of workers and the region’s automotive sector in limbo.
